---
title: "F vs Rsquared"
format: html
---

For a simple linear regression with intercept (model \(y=\beta_0+\beta_1 x+\varepsilon\)) under the classical OLS assumptions (i.i.d. normal errors), the exact distribution of \(R^2\) is induced by an F distribution.

Let \(n\) be sample size. Then
\[
F=\frac{(R^2/1)}{(1-R^2)/(n-2)} \sim F_{1,\;n-2}
\]
equivalently,
\[
\frac{R^2}{1-R^2}\cdot (n-2)\sim F_{1,\;n-2}.
\]

From this, you can express \(R^2\) directly: if the true slope is zero (\(\beta_1=0\)), then
\[
R^2 \sim \text{Beta}\!\left(\frac{1}{2},\frac{n-2}{2}\right).
\]

If \(\beta_1\neq 0\) (noncentral case), the corresponding test statistic is noncentral:
\[
F \sim F_{1,\;n-2}(\lambda),
\]
where \(\lambda\) is the noncentrality parameter determined by the effect size and design (roughly, \(\lambda\propto\beta_1^2\) times the centered \(x\)-sum of squares divided by \(\sigma^2\)). In that case, \(R^2\) follows a noncentral analog (not a simple central Beta).


## Linear Regression

$$Y\sim X$$

$$f\sim F(p, n-p-1), \quad R^2\sim Beta(p/2, (n-p-1)/2)$$
where $p$ is the number of predictors.


For a categorical $X$ with $k$ levels, $p=k-1$, and 

$$f\sim F(k-1, n-k), \quad R^2\sim Beta\left(\frac{k-1}{2}, \frac{n-k}{2}\right)$$

```{r}
suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(tidyverse)
})

dst<- mtcars |> mutate(cyl=factor(cyl), am=factor(am)) |> na.omit()

n<- nrow(dst)

mdlA <- lm(hp~wt, dst)
mdlB <- lm(hp~am, dst)
mdlC <- lm(hp~cyl, dst)

dfA1<- mdlA$df.residual
dfB1<- mdlB$df.residual
dfC1<- mdlC$df.residual

fA<- summary(mdlA)$fstatistic
fB<- summary(mdlB)$fstatistic
fC<- summary(mdlC)$fstatistic

RsqA <- summary(mdlA)$r.square
RsqB <- summary(mdlB)$r.square
RsqC <- summary(mdlC)$r.square

c(p_F=1-pf(fA[1], fA[2], fA[3]), p_Beta=1-pbeta(RsqA, fA[2]/2, fA[3]/2))
c(p_F=1-pf(fB[1], fB[2], fB[3]), p_Beta=1-pbeta(RsqB, fB[2]/2, fB[3]/2))
c(p_F=1-pf(fC[1], fC[2], fC[3]), p_Beta=1-pbeta(RsqC, fC[2]/2, fC[3]/2))

```
